claim: The study analyzed electronic health records of 14,017 patients from Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen spanning a 19 year period.
source: Text mining the electronic health records of 14,017 patients, we matched two controlled vocabularies (ICD-10 and a custom vocabulary developed at the clinical center Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen) to clinical narratives spanning a 19 year period.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of patients and time period in the abstract.

claim: The two matched vocabularies comprise over 20,000 medical terms describing symptoms, other diagnoses, and lifestyle factors.
source: The two matched vocabularies comprise over 20,000 medical terms describing symptoms, other diagnoses, and lifestyle factors.

claim: The cohort is genetically homogeneous, consisting of Caucasian diabetes patients from Denmark.
source: The cohort is genetically homogeneous (Caucasian diabetes patients from Denmark) so the resulting stratification is not driven by ethnic differences, but rather by inherently dissimilar progression patterns and lifestyle related risk factors.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the genetic homogeneity of the cohort.

claim: Using unsupervised Markov clustering, 71 clusters of at least 50 individuals were defined within the diabetes spectrum.
source: Using unsupervised Markov clustering, we defined 71 clusters of at least 50 individuals within the diabetes spectrum.

claim: The clusters display distinct and shared longitudinal glycemic dysregulation patterns.
source: The clusters display both distinct and shared longitudinal glycemic dysregulation patterns, temporal co-occurrences of comorbidities, and associations to single nucleotide polymorphisms in or near genes relevant for diabetes comorbidities.

claim: Text mining with two vocabularies resulted in a 4-fold increase in codes per patient compared to assigned codes alone.
